assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics gave a unified formal and empirical framework for how electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal institutions shape policy outcomes and growth. It changed how economists treat government as an endogenous actor rather than a benevolent planner, and it links to work on institutions and prosperity that the Committee has already recognised. The contribution is general and is cited well beyond its own subfield.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are most clearly tied to the constitutional and electoral-rule research programme and its synthesis in their monograph and papers. Besley is central to state capacity and to the political-agency and accountability literature. A three-person prize fits the core contributions, although other political-economy theorists such as Acemoglu and Robinson already have prizes and others such as Alesina are no longer available.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from the 1990s and 2000s, and the empirical tests of its predictions (for example, on electoral systems and spending) have accumulated over two decades. The field is mature and has been validated, so timing is not a constraint.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize on institutions may make the Committee reluctant to reward a neighbouring area so soon.
Identification in the cross-country constitutional evidence is weaker than in the theory, and the empirical results are contested.
Whether the prize is best framed around constitutions and electoral rules or around state capacity could change the laureate set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and credit cycles explain how small shocks are amplified and persist through asset prices and borrowing limits. The mechanism underpins most modern macro-financial modelling and the policy discussion of leverage and financial stability after 2008. It is a clear foundational mechanism with broad influence.
assessment.attribution: The Kiyotaki–Moore 'Credit Cycles' paper (1997) is the identifiable origin of the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the related financial-accelerator and empirical line, which builds on Bernanke's prior recognition. A Kiyotaki–Moore prize is the cleanest attribution and avoids diluting credit.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly three decades old, widely replicated and extended, and incorporated into central-bank models. It is mature.
uncertainties: Gertler's role in financial-accelerator and macro-financial models overlaps with the New Keynesian candidate, and excluding him from this one is a judgement call.
Some of the mechanism's empirical content rests on calibrated models rather than clean identification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Staggered pricing and wage contracts and the New Keynesian synthesis provided the standard framework for monetary policy analysis and inflation targeting. Calvo's pricing device, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's microfounded theory of policy are all widely used in central banks. The influence on practice is very large.
assessment.attribution: The list is crowded (eight names), and credit is split among theory, estimation of DSGE models and policy rules. Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are the clearest originators on pricing frictions, rules and the integrated framework. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets are important for estimation and extension but arguably follow the initial ideas.
assessment.maturity: The ideas are 30–40 years old and have been tested by policy experience, including the post-2008 and post-2021 inflation episodes. It is highly mature.
uncertainties: Recent inflation experience and the weakness of representative-agent DSGE models in forecasting create reputational uncertainty.
Priority disputes among Taylor, Calvo, Fischer, Phelps and others, and the difficulty of limiting the prize to three, make the attribution contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm models changed trade theory by explaining exporter selection, productivity effects of trade and a new channel for the gains from trade. They bridge theory and firm-level microdata, and they are used in policy evaluation. The 2008 prize for new trade theory did not cover this, so it is a distinct advance.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the seminal model. Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple, extended it to firm-level export and FDI decisions and has a long record in the trade field. Redding's contributions are more recent and quantitative, and they overlap with the quantitative trade candidate. Bernard, Eaton and Jensen also contributed to the empirical line but are not listed.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years have passed, and the framework is the workhorse of modern trade research. Empirical validation is good.
uncertainties: Omission of the empirical firm-level pioneers (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum) from this list may distort credit.
Helpman also appears under the trade-politics candidate, which could split support.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence and models of reciprocity and inequity aversion explained why people deviate from narrow self-interest in strategic settings. They reshaped incentives, contract and public goods theory and linked experimental results to formal models. The idea is influential across economics, political science and psychology.
assessment.attribution: Fehr–Schmidt (1999) is the canonical formal model, and Fehr's experimental programme provided most of the evidence. Falk contributed substantially, particularly on field evidence and preferences, but is a later contributor. Rabin, Bolton and Ockenfels offered competing formal models and are only partly recognised in this list.
assessment.maturity: The work is 25 years old and well replicated, although the stability of social preferences across contexts has been challenged.
uncertainties: Replicability and external validity of lab-based social preference evidence are debated.
Behavioural economics has had several recent prizes (Kahneman, Thaler), which may reduce room for this topic.
Rabin and others have claims on the same ideas.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run series on top incomes and wealth, built from tax data, transformed the empirical study of inequality and the public debate. The datasets are public goods used across fields, and the offshore wealth estimates changed enforcement policy. Some of the theoretical interpretations are less settled than the measurement.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez started the top-income series, and Zucman extended them to wealth and offshore holdings. The World Inequality Database involved many collaborators, including Atkinson (deceased). Credit is therefore attributable to a team, though the three names capture the main line.
assessment.maturity: Top-income work dates from about 2003 and wealth work from the 2010s, so parts are recent. The impact is large, but evaluation of the wealth-series methods is still unfolding.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of the wealth and capital-share estimates (for example, on capitalization methods and tax-data treatment) are not fully resolved.
Debate on whether the contribution is primarily measurement or the underlying economic explanation.
Political salience may make some committee members cautious.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data gave the first credible, granular measures of intergenerational mobility and of the neighbourhood and childhood-exposure effects behind it. The work is methodologically innovative and has had large influence on research and policy debates. It exemplifies a shift towards big administrative data.
assessment.attribution: Chetty leads the programme, with Hendren and Friedman key collaborators on mobility, place effects and related work. Katz contributed through the Moving to Opportunity reanalysis. The collaborative team nature makes the three-person limit awkward and may understate the many co-authors.
assessment.maturity: Most of the work is from 2014 onward and is still being evaluated. Its causal interpretation, particularly of place effects, has had replication and robustness checks only recently, so it is comparatively early.
uncertainties: Recency makes durability uncertain, and the Committee often waits longer.
Questions about causal identification of place effects and sensitivity to data choices.
Chetty also appears in the optimal-taxation candidate, and the cleanest framing of the prize is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal inference (double/debiased ML, causal forests, heterogeneous treatment effects) opened a new methodological toolkit that is now used in empirical work in many fields. It addresses high-dimensional confounding while retaining valid inference. The breadth of adoption is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov and co-authors developed double machine learning and orthogonalisation. Athey (with Wager and Imbens) developed causal forests and the policy-learning agenda. Wager is a junior collaborator on the forests. Credit is shared with others such as Imbens, who was already recognised, and Belloni, Hansen and Newey on related ideas.
assessment.maturity: The main papers date from about 2016–2018, so the field is young. Adoption is rapid but long-run value and the stability of the methods are not yet established.
uncertainties: It is probably too early for the Committee, which tends to wait for confirmation.
Overlap with the semiparametric and robust inference candidates complicates attribution.
Practical gains over simpler methods are still debated.
